executiveSynthesis: Across the two days, the notes move from building a useful information and control foundation toward defining and verifying complete work. Day 1 emphasized task-specific knowledge, active access boundaries, consequential failure tests, numerical provenance and a value baseline. Day 2 adds explicit intent and independent verification, end-to-end task success, multidimensional quality, reusable procedural skills and finance-oriented work products. The strongest wealth-management pattern is human augmentation: preparing an analysis or brief while a professional focuses elsewhere, followed by review and adjustment. These are mechanisms and hypotheses recorded from speakers; the notes do not establish autonomous advice, universal readiness, causal ROI or independently validated safety.

reportBackMessages.headline: Build around a complete, reviewable workflow rather than an impressive answer
reportBackMessages.message: Institutional information, procedural knowledge and the final work product belong together. Bridgewater's task-specific information foundation, the finance-interface discussion and the Range skills vignette point toward workflows such as a prepared meeting or a draft analysis that a professional can inspect and accept. The useful success definition includes the evidence, necessary questions, limits, edits and handoff—not just fluent generation.
reportBackMessages.evidenceBoundary: This is cross-session synthesis. Range is now identified through the user’s confirmation and official metadata, but the supplied notes provide no measured comparison showing higher advisor capacity or better client outcomes.

reportBackMessages.headline: Confidence needs preventive boundaries, independent checks and an evidence trail
reportBackMessages.message: Two Sigma's declared access and active controls, Kepler's source/calculation/citation path and Sonar's intent–guardrails–verification–evidence framework reinforce one operating principle: a person or another model agreeing with an answer is insufficient assurance. Make permitted behavior explicit, prevent defined invalid actions, and retain reviewable evidence of the checks performed.
reportBackMessages.evidenceBoundary: The frameworks and mechanisms are speaker-described. No control effectiveness, universal code-size threshold or calibrated confidence formula is established by the notes.

reportBackMessages.headline: Evaluate complete work across quality dimensions, then measure accepted value against a baseline
reportBackMessages.message: The end-to-end-evals notes, the banking session’s quality-vector framing, Sonar's judge-variability concern and Day 1's risk/value discussions argue for separate task, safety and experience measures. Inspect evaluator errors, preserve severe-failure gates, and include human review and repeated-attempt cost before interpreting productivity or business value.
reportBackMessages.evidenceBoundary: Neither average quality, pass@k, conversation volume nor adoption proves safe single-attempt completion, causal financial value or a successful rollout.

learnings.title: Specify the job, workflow and acceptable completion before building skills
learnings.synthesis: Day 1's business-value questions and Day 2's end-to-end-evals notes both start with what work must succeed. The Range financial-planning vignette adds a procedural dimension: a skill needs to know which client information is available, how to obtain it and how recommendations are prepared. Its Pick–Teach–Pack–Test–Ship sequence includes why the work is done, questions the agent must ask and limits it must respect.
practicalTips: Choose a repeatable workflow whose output a domain expert can judge.
Record required inputs, why each step matters, mandatory questions, limits, handoff and acceptance criteria.
Judge the completed work product and correction effort, not only whether an agent produced an answer.
learnings.limit: Range attribution is confirmed, but the notes supply no measured result. The five steps are a recorded workflow idea, not a verified industry standard or evidence of suitability for autonomous advice.

learnings.title: Evaluate the model, context, skills and memory as one task system
learnings.synthesis: Bridgewater distinguishes information needs by consumer and task. The Day 2 eval notes then describe experiments with skill ablation, reducing an eight-skill bundle to four, trajectory-distilled memory and a smaller spreadsheet skill. Together, they suggest that more context or more skills should earn their place through a controlled end-to-end comparison.
practicalTips: Hold the representative task set and grading rubric constant while varying one component where feasible.
Measure task acceptance, consequential errors, latency, cost and reviewer effort together.
Distinguish partial-credit task quality from binary success and repeated-attempt measures such as pass@k.
learnings.limit: The notes say the experiments worked but give no effect sizes, task set, model versions, costs or statistical uncertainty. Eight-to-four is a reported configuration change, not a recommended bundle size.

learnings.title: Use prevention and independent verification together
learnings.synthesis: Day 1's registered access boundaries and numerical-evidence checks align with Sonar's confidence framing: explicit intent, guardrails, independent verification and repeatable evidence. Prevention reduces defined invalid behavior; verification checks what actually happened. Neither eliminates the need for accountable judgment on unresolved cases.
practicalTips: State the allowed resources, actions, output requirements and escalation conditions before execution.
Choose checks that fail differently from the generator; verify inputs and transformations as well as presentation.
Retain enough versioned evidence to repeat a check and understand an exception.
learnings.limit: Sonar's multiplication is a conceptual framework, not a calibrated confidence probability. The notes do not establish how independent any particular verification implementation was or what failure coverage it achieved.

learnings.title: Keep safety, task success and user experience visible as separate dimensions
learnings.synthesis: The Day 1 failure study argues that frequency alone misses consequential harm. The banking-session Day 2 notes call quality a vector and distinguish safety, task and experience measures. This provides a way to expose tradeoffs rather than allowing a high overall score to hide a critical failure or poor user experience.
practicalTips: Keep separate measures for prohibited behavior, task completion, coverage/completeness and experience.
Define critical-failure conditions explicitly instead of averaging them into a satisfaction score.
Review quality by task and failure category; high volume can conceal important rare cases.
learnings.limit: The notes contain an ambiguous safety term ('roundedness') and no operational definitions for satisfaction or knowledge retention. They do not specify thresholds, measured quality or bank identity.

learnings.title: Treat automated judges and human review as fallible parts of the system
learnings.synthesis: Two Sigma's selective-approval classifier and the Day 1 harm-detection discussion become more concrete in Day 2: Sonar raises variable judge answers and cognitive surrender, while the banking session suggests a judge that tends toward failing and is part of configuration. The synthesis is to calibrate oversight, rather than assuming either a human or a stricter model is automatically reliable.
practicalTips: Compare judge decisions with independently adjudicated examples, including severe false passes and unnecessary false failures.
Version judge model, prompt, rubric and threshold with the evaluated system.
Use repeat assessments to inspect variability and examine whether reviewers meaningfully challenge unsupported outputs.
learnings.limit: Fail-leaning grading is a speaker proposal, not a demonstrated optimum. It can increase false rejections and review burden. The notes do not quantify cognitive surrender or establish that all human review fails to scale.

learnings.title: Make financial work products inspectable at the point of use
learnings.synthesis: Kepler's claim-level numerical evidence connects to the OpenAI session's finance-oriented interface, source passages/tables/charts and document/artifact generation. The Range vignette places a professional's review, editing and adjustment at the end of an analysis workflow. This suggests treating the final brief, spreadsheet or presentation as a decision surface with accessible evidence, not merely a formatted answer.
practicalTips: Keep source passages, tables, calculation lineage and relevant dates accessible beside consequential claims.
Distinguish sourced data, computed figures, assumptions and professional judgment in a final artifact.
Evaluate whether a reviewer can find and correct an error efficiently, including after an artifact is exported.
learnings.limit: These are described capabilities and proposed design implications. The notes do not establish feature availability, firm-specific entitlements, provider integrations, data coverage, citation correctness or artifact accuracy. Do not infer provider identities from uncertain spellings.

learnings.title: Measure capacity and value after review costs and consequences are included
learnings.synthesis: The Range vignette describes parallel preparation—an agent drafts another client's analysis while a planner is on a call—followed by human review. Contour's counterfactual/value questions and Capital One's lifespan/dependency discussion help assess that proposition: generating work cheaply matters only when the output is useful, reviewable and worth maintaining or safely retiring.
practicalTips: Measure accepted analyses or prepared meetings per professional, total human time and output quality against the existing process.
Include retries, review, corrections, exception handling and operating costs when estimating capacity gains.
Separate professional capacity from client outcomes, sales, financial return and autonomous decision authority.
learnings.limit: The Range vignette is an unverified speaker account, not proof of higher advisor throughput, better advice or incremental revenue. Sonar’s claims about compounding errors and long-running work motivate testing, not a universal task-length limit.

ambiguitiesAndCaveats.treatment: The notes do not define the metric. Partial-credit grading and at-least-one-success across multiple attempts answer different questions. A high pass@k does not establish first-attempt reliability; include all attempts' cost and the method used to choose a usable output.
